comment: After the second paragraph the post loses its thread: it lists options and tools, then jumps straight to "To test how accurate..." and a run of three percentages. Nothing says why the test mattered, so the reader's attention drops. Each paragraph should follow from the one before: why the test was needed, what was tested, what the result means (with the number inside the sentence), and the decision it led to.

Rejected. 1) Media: no graphs at all. The document pages repeat the post's own sentences (question in large type, answer in small type) and the results page is a list of numbers. Every page must be a chart of the story's data; never restate post text as media. 2) Text: it opens on a bare result ('A contract risk model reached 86.20% accuracy...') with no setting. Say first what the project is and what problem it solves, for whom, then the result. 3) It ends on a question; end with one plain sentence on what the work now lets someone do.

rules: unsupported by the facts: Claim that predicting cancellations 'improved' with a new model (FACTS describe building a new model, not improving an existing one).

unsupported by the facts: Causal link between the model's good ROC-AUC and the decision to deploy it (FACTS state both the ROC-AUC and the deployment decision, but do not explicitly state that the ROC-AUC was the reason for the deployment).
unsupported by the facts: Claim that reliably detecting sensor spikes and preventing device failures without false alarms was 'the engineering challenge'.

comment: Rejected for the image only. The card showed two bare numbers (232, 210) instead of a chart because the post's 98.13% / 90.52% did not match the stored 0.9813 / 0.9052. Fixed in eda6b42: rates now chart as bars in the post's own notation. The text was acceptable: setting first, no closing question, all numbers from the facts. Keep the same story and that shape.

rules: unsupported by the facts: Claim that testing tiny adapters on LLMs is the fastest way to see real impact.
unsupported by the facts: Motivation statement that the LoRA experiment was needed to fit on a free Colab T4 GPU.
unsupported by the facts: Assertion that the author can now reliably test a LoRA adapter on a small synthetic set and know exactly which types of prompts it will affect before any production use.
reading flow: Opening claim about speed (“fastest way to see real impact”) is presented without supporting explanation.
reading flow: Conclusion that the adapter can be reliably tested and its effect on prompt types known before production jumps from a five‑prompt test without a clear logical bridge.
unsupported by the facts: States a motivation: needed a way to test without rebuilding the whole model – not mentioned in the facts.
unsupported by the facts: Describes the dataset as "synthetic" – the facts only say a 600‑example subset, not that it was synthetic.
unsupported by the facts: Claims the adapter is "cheap" and can be attached to steer creative generation while preserving factual consistency – the facts do not mention cost or deployment capability.

unsupported by the facts: Claims that researchers can now refresh the Tableau report in under seven seconds and trust that the underlying data remain unchanged, which is not stated in the provided facts.
unsupported by the facts: Claims "perfect reliability" which is not supported by the facts (facts only show 124/124 successes, not absolute perfection).
unsupported by the facts: Mentions personal motivation (“I needed to prove…”) which is not present in the provided facts

comment: Rejected. 1) Image: daily returns (-2.58%, -1.2%) drawn as near-empty bars on a 0-100% axis; returns are changes, not shares. Fixed in b452d93: the shared measure (each day's Z-score) is charted as bars. 2) Text: 140 words, under the 150 minimum; the draft check split hyphenated words and counted it as 150+. Fixed in b452d93. 3) 'The detector marked the spike and ignored the flat series' and 'insights' are not in the facts. Keep the setting-first opening and the plain ending.

rules: 144 words, must be at least 150: add about 21 words using only details the facts already give (how the test was set up, each result and what it means, what the decision changed); never add a reason or benefit the facts do not state
